study.title: Judges 1 - Incomplete conquest and partial fidelity of Israel
study.overview: Judges 1 describes the period after Joshua's death and shows how the tribes of Israel began the occupation of the land, but did not complete it. The chapter alternates between victories granted by God and persistent failures in expelling the Canaanites. Judah and Simeon advance with courage, Caleb appears as an example of faith and reward, the Naurians join Israel, but several tribes let Canaanites remain among them. The result is a picture of real yet incomplete obedience and a gradual coexistence with the threat that God had commanded to remove.

outline.title: Consultation to the Lord and first victories of Judah
outline.explanation: After the death of Joshua, Israel seeks God's direction over who is to begin the struggle. The Lord chooses Judah, which counts on Simeon. Together they defeat the Canaanites and the Perizeites at Bezek, capture Adoni-Bezek and take Jerusalem. The episode shows human initiative subordinated to the divine word and already introduces the theme of partial conquest.

outline.title: Advancement in Judah, Caleb's courage and the blessing of Achsa
outline.explanation: Judah continues the campaign against peoples in the mountains, the south and the plains. Hebron and Debir come on the scene, and Caleb's bounty for Debir leads to Otniel's marriage to Acsa. Acsa's request for water sources reveals practical wisdom and dependence on provision for the received land.

outline.title: The Kenyans and new victories with limits
outline.explanation: The sons of the Native son, connected to the family of Moses, come to dwell between Judah. Judah and Simeon also defeat Zephath, and take Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ekron, and the text states that the Lord was with Judah. Even so, Judah cannot drive out those who live in the plains because of the iron cars, showing that the divine presence does not automatically eliminate any difficulty when there are human limits in advance.

outline.title: Concessions, coexistence and repeated failure of tribes
outline.explanation: Benjamin does not cast out the Jebusites out of Jerusalem; the house of Joseph takes Bethel through a stratagem, but allows the man of the city to establish another Light. Then Manasseh, Ephraim, Zebulun, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan also did not utterly cast out the Canaanites. In several cases, the remaining peoples become tributaries or come to live in the midst of Israel. The chapter ends with the Amoria pressure and a border still marked by the enemy presence.

study.context: The chapter lies after the death of Joshua and, according to the notes, it seems to occur at a time relatively close to this event. The emphasis falls less on chronological details and more on the leadership transition: Israel no longer counts on Joshua and needs to consult the Lord to guide his campaigns. The text also works as a complement to previous accounts of land occupation, recording both progress and failure.
study.theology: Judges 1 teaches that the conquest of the earth depends on the word and presence of God, but also exposes human responsibility to obey in a complete way. The Lord directs, gives victory, and accompanies Judah, but Israel does not always persevere to the end. The chapter shows that half obedience produces coexistence with sin and the threat: instead of totally expelling the Canaanite peoples, several tribes tolerate them, subordinate them or live alongside them. Retributive justice also appears in the case of Adoni-Bezeque, although the text does not present this as a mechanical rule, but as a recognition of his own wickedness. At the same time, there are signs of grace and provision, such as the faithfulness of Caleb, the inheritance given to his daughter, and the acceptance of the keones among the people of God.

scholarViews.insight: Matthew Henry points out that Judah and Simeon carried out successful campaigns, but the men of Judah failed before the iron chariots, and this retreat weakened the example they could have given to the other tribes.
Adam Clarke notes that the Naanites, descendants of Moses' father-in-law, were always linked to Israel and that the expression "city of the palm trees" probably refers to a place near Jericho.

questions: In which areas do I seek the direction of the Lord, but I still let a partial obedience replace complete obedience?
Which Nacananeus remain around me because I tolerate them, instead of facing them with faith and firmness?
How can I, like Achsa, ask God concrete resources to live fruitfully in the inheritance he has given me?
study.practice: Read the chapter as a spiritual mirror: identify where there is real courage and where there are concessions. Pray that God may give him not only initial victories, but perseverance to the end. Make a practical decision this week to cut an area of coexistence with sin, a relationship with lies, or a habit that you already know should not maintain. At the same time, imitate Caleb and Achsa: ask God for specific provision to serve better in what he has already entrusted to him.
study.uncertainty: The chapter does not accurately inform the date or the duration between Joshua's death and these events. The notes suggest some likely identifications, such as the location of the "city of palm trees" and the interpretation of certain names, but these are interpretive readings and cannot be treated as explicit facts of the text. It is also not possible to affirm with certainty to what extent all the actions described occurred exactly in the order or in the same period in which they are narrated.
